title: A Dispassionate Review of Roe v Wade
summary: Josh and Chuck take a dispassionate look at the 1973 Supreme Court case Roe v. Wade. They cover the history of abortion law in the US from the 19th century, the AMA campaign and the quickening and viability standards, and the central unresolved question of when life begins. They profile Norma McCorvey (Jane Roe), the lawyers Linda Coffee and Sarah Weddington, and the mootness ruling. They trace precedent cases (United States v. Vuitch, Meyer v. Nebraska, Pierce v. Society of Sisters, Griswold v. Connecticut) that led to substantive due process and a right to privacy. They discuss companion cases Doe v. Bolton and John and Mary Doe, the majority opinion, the Turnaway Study, strict scrutiny, the trimester framework, Planned Parenthood v. Casey and its undue burden standard, and the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe. The episode closes with criticism of the confirmation hearings and the Court's legitimacy, and a listener mail segment about "don't yuck someone's yum."

segments.title: Introduction and overview of Roe v. Wade
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, describe Roe v. Wade (1973) as a sweeping ruling that struck down most state abortion bans, and give a brief history of abortion regulation in the US, including the AMA campaign and the terminology debate over pro-life and pro-choice.

segments.title: When life begins and the quickening and viability standards
segments.summary: The hosts explain that no consensus exists on when life begins. They describe quickening as an early regulatory marker and viability as the later standard, and quote the Court saying it cannot speculate on when life technically begins.

segments.title: Norma McCorvey, Jane Roe, and the attorneys
segments.summary: Jane Roe is identified as Norma McCorvey, a Texas woman who wanted an abortion that Texas law did not allow. Attorneys Linda Coffee and Sarah Weddington took her case. McCorvey later became pro-life and said she was manipulated and paid to change sides. The hosts also mention the film Citizen Ruth.

segments.title: Mootness, standing, and the Court's composition
segments.summary: The hosts explain how McCorvey's child had already been born and adopted, which raised a mootness problem. The Court ruled that pregnancy is capable of repetition yet evading review, so the case was not moot. They also describe the justice changes in 1971 (Black, Harlan, Blackmun, Powell, Rehnquist) that delayed the rehearing.
topics: capable of repetition yet evading review

segments.title: Precedent cases: US v. Vuitch, Meyer, Pierce, Griswold
segments.summary: The hosts cover earlier cases that shaped Roe: United States v. Vuitch, where the Court upheld DC's abortion law and noted that health could include psychological health; Meyer v. Nebraska and Pierce v. Society of Sisters, which shaped how the Ninth and Fourteenth Amendments were read; and Griswold v. Connecticut, which established a right to privacy and substantive due process, which the hosts call a legal fiction.

segments.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg's critique and the privacy foundation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why Roe was on shaky legal ground because it rested on privacy rather than the Constitution's text. They note that Ruth Bader Ginsburg thought it should have been argued under the Equal Protection Clause, and mention Loving v. Virginia as an earlier privacy-related case.

segments.title: Companion cases and Doe v. Bolton
segments.summary: The hosts describe the roughly eighteen related cases, including John and Mary Doe over birth control and James Hallford, and Doe v. Bolton, a Georgia case with procedural hurdles. The Court ruled 7-2 in both Roe and Doe v. Bolton.

segments.title: The majority opinion and the Turnaway Study
segments.summary: The hosts summarize the majority reasoning on health, stress, and stigma. They then describe the Turnaway Study, which found that women denied abortions had worse outcomes, and a follow-up study that checked its methodology.

segments.title: Strict scrutiny, the trimester framework, and viability
segments.summary: The hosts explain strict scrutiny and compare it to gun rights under the Second Amendment. They describe Roe's trimester framework, the arbitrary nature of it given medical advances in viability, and how this led to challenges.

segments.title: Planned Parenthood v. Casey and undue burden
segments.summary: The hosts cover Planned Parenthood v. Casey, a plurality decision that upheld most of a Pennsylvania law, struck spousal notification, dropped the trimester framework for viability, and introduced the undue burden standard, which opened the way for more restrictive state laws.

segments.title: Dobbs decision, confirmation controversy, and Court legitimacy
segments.summary: The hosts report that Dobbs overturned Roe and returned the question to states. They discuss criticism of Justices Kavanaugh and Gorsuch's confirmation testimony, the electoral college issue, the Garland and Barrett confirmation timing, concerns about privacy-based rulings such as gay marriage, and the hosts' call for term limits.

segments.title: Listener mail: don't yuck someone's yum
segments.summary: A listener from England says her young daughters and childminder picked up the saying 'don't yuck someone's yum' from the show, and it spread to other families. The hosts thank listener Matt Walford.
